text: Welcome. By the end of this deck you'll be running your own private AI chatbot, entirely on your own PC, with nothing sent to the cloud. We'll go through Windows Subsystem for Linux, Ollama, and OpenWebUI, one exact command at a time. No prior Linux experience needed.

Here's the shape of the journey. First we install Windows Subsystem for Linux. Then we install Ollama inside it and learn its core commands. Next we pick an AI model sized right for your computer. And finally we install OpenWebUI, so you get a clean chat window in your browser instead of a bare terminal.

A quick reality check before we start. You'll need Windows 10 build 19041 or later, or Windows 11, both 64-bit, with virtualization turned on in your BIOS — it usually is by default. Plan on 8 gigabytes of RAM as a floor, 16 or more if you want to run bigger models comfortably, and about 20 gigabytes of free disk space to get through this whole walkthrough.

Let's define our first term. W-S-L stands for Windows Subsystem for Linux. It's a genuine Linux environment that runs directly inside Windows — no virtual machine to babysit, no dual-boot, no second computer. Files and networking are shared between the two sides, and this is where Ollama is actually going to live.

Here's the install, step by step. Open PowerShell as Administrator — right-click the Start button and choose Terminal, Admin. Then run one command: w-s-l space dash dash install. Restart when Windows asks you to. Ubuntu will finish setting itself up automatically and open a window asking you to create a Linux username and password — this is separate from your Windows login, so pick anything you'll remember. Once that's done, you're looking at a real Linux terminal running inside Windows.
This is what that install looks like in practice — PowerShell downloading the WSL2 kernel and Ubuntu, followed by that first-boot prompt for your new Linux username and password.

A handful of commands cover almost everything you'll need day to day. w-s-l space dash-l space dash-v lists your installed distros. Just w-s-l on its own drops you straight into Ubuntu. w-s-l dash-dash shutdown fully stops everything if something gets stuck. dash-dash update keeps the engine itself current. And dash-dash version tells you exactly what you're running.

Running wsl dash-l dash-v confirms two things at a glance: that Ubuntu is installed, and that it's on version 2 — which is what you want. If it says version 1, something's off and it's worth re-running the installer.

Next term: Ollama. It's a free tool that downloads, runs, and manages AI language models directly on your own computer — no cloud account, no subscription, no API key to sign up for. Everything happens locally, which means your prompts never leave your machine.

Installing Ollama inside WSL is one line. Open your Ubuntu terminal, then run: curl space dash f-s-s-capital L space the address https colon slash slash ollama dot com slash install dot s-h, piped to s-h. Let it finish — it sets Ollama up to run as a background service automatically. Confirm it worked with ollama space dash dash version.

Here's that install script running — it drops the ollama binary into place and starts the background service listening on port eleven-four-three-four, which is the address every Ollama command talks to under the hood.

This is the whole cheat sheet. pull just downloads a model. run downloads it if needed and immediately starts a chat. list shows everything you've got on disk; p-s shows what's actually loaded in memory right now. show gives you details on one model. And rm deletes a model for good, while stop just frees the memory without deleting anything.

Model choice comes down to your hardware, not preference. llama3.2 at 3 billion parameters is small, fast, and fine on 8 gigabytes of RAM — great for testing. Mistral 7B or llama3.1 8B is the balanced middle ground, and honestly the sensible default if you've got 16 gigabytes. The 70 billion parameter version of llama3.1 is genuinely better, but it wants 64 gigabytes of RAM or a real GPU — don't try it on a laptop.

Let's actually run one. ollama space pull space llama3 point 2 downloads it. Once the progress bars finish, ollama space run space llama3 point 2 drops you straight into a chat — type a question, hit Enter, and the model answers right there in the terminal. When you're done, type slash bye to exit cleanly.
This is what that first conversation looks like — a simple triple-arrow prompt waiting for your question, with the model's answer streaming back word by word, right there in the terminal.

Last piece of vocabulary: OpenWebUI. It's a private, browser-based chat interface for whatever models Ollama is running — it looks and feels a lot like ChatGPT, except it's entirely yours, running entirely on your own machine.

OpenWebUI runs inside a Docker container, so Docker Desktop comes first. Download it from docker dot com, run the installer, and keep the “Use WSL 2” option checked. Restart when it asks. Once Docker Desktop is open and shows Running in the corner, go to Settings, Resources, WSL Integration, and turn the toggle on for Ubuntu. Click Apply and Restart to lock it in.
This toggle is the one setting that trips people up if it's missed — without it, Docker can't see your WSL environment at all. Flip it on for Ubuntu and you're set.

This one docker run command does the whole job. The dash-p flag opens the interface at localhost port 3000. add-host lets the container reach out and find Ollama running on your WSL host. The dash-v flag saves your chat history so it survives restarts. And restart-always means it comes back on its own after a reboot, so you're not re-running this command every time.
A quick docker space p-s confirms the container is actually up, with port 3000 mapped and ready — that's your green light to open a browser.

Open any browser and go to localhost colon 3000. Click Sign Up — the very first account created on a fresh install automatically becomes the admin. Fill in a name, email, and password; this account is entirely local, nothing leaves your machine. Click Create Account and you land straight in the chat interface.
Here's that first-run sign-up screen — simple, and the account you create right here is automatically your admin account, no extra setup step required.

And here's the payoff — the same llama3.2 model you ran from the terminal earlier, now sitting behind a proper chat window. The dropdown at the top lists every model ollama list would show you, and you can switch between them mid-conversation.

A few snags cover almost every problem people hit. If ollama isn't found, just close and reopen your terminal. If OpenWebUI shows no models, check ollama list inside WSL first. If the page won't load, confirm Docker Desktop actually shows the container running. If things feel sluggish, wsl dash-dash shutdown and reopen gives you a clean restart. And if a model won't load at all, it's probably too big for your RAM — step down to a smaller one.

That's the whole path — WSL gave you a real Linux environment inside Windows, Ollama gave you the models and the commands to run them, and OpenWebUI gave you a proper chat window in your browser. Every command in this deck is yours to revisit any time, and none of it ever needs the cloud. Thanks for following along.
